readerTitle: Why one wrong box beats a chart full of errors
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (물류센터, 배관 서비스 회사) + 실제 연구 (Small, Loewenstein & Slovic, 2007)
insight: 사람은 평균이 아니라 한 사람의 구체적인 순간을 보고 움직인다. 리더는 숫자 앞에 진짜이고 대표적인 이야기 하나를 둔다.
misconception: 이야기는 꾸밈이고, 데이터만 정확하면 사람들이 알아서 행동을 바꾼다.

sources.text: Small, D. A., Loewenstein, G., & Slovic, P. (2007). Sympathy and callousness: The impact of deliberative thought on donations to identifiable and statistical victims. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 102(2), 143–153.
물류센터와 배관 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Small 외(2007) 연구: 말리의 7세 소녀 Rokia 이야기를 읽은 참가자가 아프리카 기아 통계를 읽은 참가자보다 약 두 배 많이 기부했다는 결과. 원문의 평균 기부액(약 $2.38 vs $1.14)을 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "about twice as much"로만 적었습니다.
같은 연구에서 이야기와 통계를 함께 보여주면 이야기만 보여줬을 때보다 기부가 줄었다는 결과가 있습니다. 원문의 해당 실험 조건을 확인하세요.
물류센터와 배관 회사의 결과(오출고 감소, 고객 반응)는 모두 가상입니다. 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Same message. Same week. Different result.
body: Two warehouse managers had the same job: get their teams to double-check every order before it ships.
One showed a chart. The room nodded, and nothing changed. The other told the team about one box. Within a week, people were checking each other's orders.

image.label: Two team huddles: one facing a chart, one leaning in to listen
image.brief: 창고 안 두 팀의 아침 조회를 좌우로 나란히. 왼쪽은 화이트보드 막대그래프 앞에서 팔짱 낀 직원들, 오른쪽은 상자 하나를 든 매니저 쪽으로 몸을 기울인 직원들. 실제 회사 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: You get five minutes at tomorrow's shift meeting.
body: You run a distribution center that supplies small hardware stores. Wrong items in orders have crept up this quarter. You want every picker to scan twice before sealing a box.

options.text: Show the error rate and what each mistake costs the company
options.feedback: Accurate and quick. But a percentage feels like nobody in particular, so few people feel it's about their own boxes.

options.text: Tell what happened to one customer who got a wrong order, then show the number
options.feedback: The story makes the problem feel real. The number that follows proves it isn't a one-off. You spend a minute more and gain attention.

options.text: Announce the new rule and what happens if people skip it
options.feedback: Clear and fast. But people follow rules they understand, and a rule without a reason invites quiet shortcuts.

cards.title: The chart and the box.
body: At the first warehouse, the manager put up a chart: errors up this quarter, with a cost per mistake. People agreed it was bad. Then they went back to picking the way they always had.

At the second, the manager held up a box. "A store owner opened this on Saturday morning. A contractor was waiting at his counter for these parts. They were the wrong size. He lost the sale, and he called us angry."
Then she showed the same chart. This time, people asked how to stop it.

image.label: A store owner opening a box of wrong parts while a contractor waits
image.brief: 작은 철물점 카운터. 주인이 상자를 열고 당황한 표정, 맞은편에 작업복 입은 시공업자가 시계를 보며 기다림. 따뜻한 일러스트 톤, 실제 브랜드 표시 없음.

cards.title: Storytelling for leaders
body: **Storytelling for leaders** means making your point through a short, true account of a specific person facing a problem, and what changed.
It isn't entertainment. It gives people something they can picture. A chart tells them *that* something matters. A story shows them *who* it matters to, so they can see their own part in it.

cards.title: One girl moved people more than millions.
body: In a 2007 study, researchers Deborah Small, George Loewenstein and Paul Slovic asked people to donate to a children's charity.
Some read about Rokia, a seven-year-old girl in Mali. Others read statistics about millions of hungry children across Africa. The Rokia group gave **about twice as much**.
A twist: when the statistics were shown next to Rokia's story, giving dropped. Numbers alone can make people calculate instead of care. So lead with the person, then use the number as proof.

cards.title: A leader's story has four parts.
body: It works for announcing a change, explaining a value or giving praise.
list: **One person:** a named customer or colleague, not "our clients"
**One moment:** a specific time and place
**The turn:** what went wrong, or what changed
**The point:** what you want people to do now
cards.callout: If it takes more than a minute, it's too long.
cards.softwareNote: In a software company, read one real support ticket aloud before showing churn numbers. A user who lost a day's work is easier to act on than a 3% churn rate.

cards.title: A story can mislead as easily as it can help.
body: Because stories work so well, one unusual case can push a team in the wrong direction. Pick a story that is typical, and check that it's true.
Never make one up or stretch it. If your team finds out, they'll doubt your next message too. And protect privacy: get permission or leave out names that customers wouldn't want shared.

cards.title: Now it's a plumbing company.
body: You own a plumbing business with eight technicians. You want every tech to give customers a written price before starting work. Some techs think it wastes time.
How do you make the case at Monday's meeting?

options.text: Share how many online reviews mention surprise bills
options.feedback: Real and relevant. But a count of reviews is easy to shrug off as "other techs, not me."

options.text: Read one real customer's complaint about a surprise bill, with permission, then show how often it happens
options.feedback: The customer's own words make it personal. The count shows it's a pattern. It costs you a phone call to ask permission.

options.text: Combine several complaints into one dramatic story told as if it were one customer
options.feedback: It might land harder in the moment. But if a tech recognizes the pieces, your credibility takes the hit, not the story.

cards.title: Lead with one true person. Then show the number.
body: People act when they can picture who a problem hurts. The number proves it's not a one-off.
**Try it today:** think of the next change you need your team to make. Write down one real customer or colleague it affects, in four lines: person, moment, turn, point.
